title: Tasks Span Too Many Screens Or Steps
summary: This workflow failure occurs when routine tasks are structurally elongated by unnecessary screen transitions, section switching, or navigation depth. It commonly appears when information architecture follows internal system modules, when users must collect related information across multiple locations, or when frequently used functions are buried too deeply.
keyFacts: Every screen crossing creates a navigation, reorientation, location, and resumption cost for the user.
The failure is usually structural rather than feature-based: the system may contain the required information but place it across too many screens or modules.
One mechanism is information architecture that follows development modules, database entities, or system sections rather than user tasks.
A second mechanism is multi-location information collection, where users must gather related values from several separate system locations and hold earlier values in memory.
A third mechanism is a mismatch between navigation depth and function frequency, where frequently used functions are buried as if they were rare configuration tasks.
In the WCO IPM case, inspection workflows crossed separate areas for case management, intelligence records, rights holder data, and inspection recording.
WCO reported a 78% reduction in training costs based on reduced training hours and a 20% increase in platform use; these were client-reported outcomes.
In the IDEXX Animana case, field research across 35 clinics in three countries documented multi-window workflows for multi-pet households and repeated section switching during consultations.
In the Elsner Cala Touch KNX case, some commonly used functions required up to 10 swipes on a device used approximately 25 times per day.

AIT and Oceaneering evidence illustrates design reasoning about avoiding unnecessary extra windows, excessive taps, and inconsistent editing flows, but it does not establish measured time-saving outcomes.

bodySections.heading: Definition: Tasks Span Too Many Screens Or Steps
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Tasks span too many screens or steps when a user must cross more screen, section, or interaction boundaries than the task itself warrants, usually because the system is organised around its internal structure rather than the user's operational task flow.

The user must navigate, reorient, locate the relevant element, and resume work at every crossing. This failure is usually not caused by missing features. It is caused by information architecture that follows the system's internal structure instead of the user's task structure.

bodySections.heading: Failure Pattern: Navigation Depth Exceeds Task Depth
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Tasks spanning too many screens or steps is a structural elongation of work. A task that operationally requires one coherent flow is broken into several screen visits, section switches, or sequential steps because the system exposes its internal architecture to the user.

A single screen crossing may not appear serious enough to report. The accumulated effect is different. Every user repeats the same small navigation tax across routine work: move to another area, rebuild context, find the relevant field, remember the previous value or state, and resume the task.

The visible symptom is often a diffuse sense that the system is slow or difficult rather than a complaint about a specific button or page. The underlying issue is that task boundaries and system boundaries do not match.

bodySections.heading: How This Failure Differs From Adjacent Workflow And Cognitive Failures
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Tasks spanning too many screens or steps is distinct from the cognitive failure in which too much attention is required for routine use. Excessive screen crossings are one structural source of navigation overhead, decision load, and reorientation effort. The cognitive cost and the structural cause are connected, but they are not the same failure.

This failure is also distinct from the workflow failure in which the system fights the user task. A system fights the task when the system's logic actively works against what the user is trying to do. A system can require too many steps for a simple task without actively resisting the task. Conversely, a system can resist the task without adding many screen crossings.

The design response differs. Excessive screen crossings require information architecture and workflow restructuring. Active task resistance requires resolving a deeper conflict between system logic and operational logic.

bodySections.heading: Information Architecture Follows System Structure Instead Of Task Structure
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The most common mechanism behind tasks spanning too many screens or steps is information architecture organised around the entities and modules the development team built. Users then have to navigate across those modules whenever the task requires information that the architecture stores separately.

An inspection workflow may require shipment data, intelligence records, and outcome recording. If those areas are separated into different system modules, the officer must cross each boundary in sequence even when the operational task requires the information together.

This pattern is a predictable result of designing from the inside out. Development teams understand a system by what it contains: user management, case management, records, configuration, reports. Users understand the same system by the work they are trying to complete. When the information architecture follows the development structure, the user performs the integration work manually through navigation.

bodySections.heading: Multi-Location Information Collection Creates Memory And Sequencing Load
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Multi-location information collection occurs when a task requires related information from several separate locations in the system. The user must visit each location, hold earlier values in memory, collect later values, and synthesise the set into a complete picture.

The documented examples include multi-pet households in a veterinary practice management system, multi-location screen deployments in a digital signage platform, and multi-invoice debtors in a financial portal. In each case, the system organises information by entity while the task requires an operational grouping across entities.

This mechanism is especially costly when the user's work is time-pressured or concurrent. A veterinary receptionist handling an incoming call and updating records for a multi-pet household cannot operationally treat the task as several isolated sequential screen visits. The navigation structure imposes a sequential constraint on work that needs to be handled as one operational situation.

bodySections.heading: Frequent Functions Are Buried At Depths Calibrated For Rare Use
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Navigation depth becomes a workflow failure when functions used many times per day are placed deep in a hierarchy. The user may pass through three, four, or five levels to reach a function used in every session.

This happens when navigation depth is based on the system's structural classification rather than function frequency. A function may be labelled as advanced configuration because of how the software is organised, while real users access it as a daily operational control.

This form is directly measurable. The number of interaction steps required to reach the function can be counted, and the operational frequency of the function can be compared against that depth.

bodySections.heading: How Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design Method Addresses Excessive Task-Spanning
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method addresses excessive task-spanning by establishing task architecture before information architecture decisions are made. Domain learning and microtask analysis document what users actually do, what information they need, in what order, and under what operational constraints.

In the WCO IPM engagement, Creative Navy documented the inspection workflow in operational terms before deciding where information should appear. The workflow established the information architecture requirement: shipment data, relevant intelligence, and inspection recording needed to be available together at the moment of inspection.

In the Elsner Cala Touch KNX engagement, Creative Navy applied the same principle to navigation frequency. The design work mapped interaction frequency to navigation depth: functions used frequently were placed closer to the surface, while rarely used functions could remain deeper.

The principle is that information architecture follows task architecture, not system architecture. System architecture is not a sufficient proxy for the sequence, grouping, or frequency of real operational work.

bodySections.heading: WCO IPM Evidence: Inspection Work Crossed Misaligned Architecture
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
IPM is a customs intelligence platform operated by the World Customs Organization for intellectual property enforcement across member administrations. The core operational act was inspection: a frontline officer checked a shipment against available intelligence and recorded the outcome.

The IPM interface had been organised around internal system architecture, with separate sections for case management, intelligence records, rights holder data, and inspection recording. The inspection workflow required several of these areas in sequence, so frontline officers had to complete several screen transitions and frequent section switching.

The difficulty was distributed across the workflow rather than located in one screen. Frontline officers described the interface as difficult and slow as a workflow. Parallel workarounds, including spreadsheets and email chains alongside the official system, indicated that some officers experienced the navigation cost as higher than the benefit of using the system for some tasks.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method rebuilt the information architecture around inspection and case management flows documented during Sandbox Experiments. Context-aware data presentation gave inspection officers access to relevant intelligence when opening a shipment record, without requiring navigation to the sections where that information was architecturally managed.

WCO reported a 78% reduction in training costs for officers and a 20% increase in platform use. These were client-reported outcomes; the 78% figure was based on reduced training hours. Usability testing with 47 participants across five countries confirmed that workflows were faster and less error-prone under realistic conditions, but the available evidence does not provide measured task-time figures.

bodySections.heading: IDEXX Animana Evidence: Multi-Window Veterinary Workflows Crossed Role And Entity Boundaries
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
IDEXX Animana is a veterinary practice management platform with eleven years of accumulated feature additions. Field research across 35 clinics in three countries documented a workflow failure in which multi-pet households required navigation across multiple windows.

A client with four pets could require one pet's appointment handling, billing questions about another pet, and prescription renewal for a third. The receptionist had to maintain multiple open records, switch between them, gather information, hold earlier context in memory, and respond to the client without the system organising the situation around the operational workflow.

Consultation documentation produced a related pattern. Recording information about the current case required repeated section switching during the consultation, including navigation away from the consultation record and then back again.

The formal usability findings from the 150+ participant, three-country field programme treated these as structural properties of the platform. The pattern appeared across first-week users and ten-year veterans. Experienced users had absorbed the overhead as habitual workflow cost, which means lack of complaint did not indicate absence of friction.

bodySections.heading: Elsner Cala Touch KNX Evidence: Common Functions Were Too Deep For Daily Interaction Frequency
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The Elsner Cala Touch KNX is a wall-mounted smart home and building automation controller for heating, cooling, lighting, blinds, and scene control in residential and commercial environments. Normal use involved approximately 25 interactions per day.

Before redesign, reaching certain commonly used functions required up to 10 swipes. The problem was not the existence of the functions. The problem was that a device used briefly and frequently placed some common actions at a depth disproportionate to their operational simplicity and frequency.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method established the navigation architecture by mapping interaction frequency directly to navigation depth. Functions accessed frequently were positioned closer to the surface; functions accessed rarely remained accessible deeper in the structure.

A formal usability test with 12 subjects confirmed that navigation and temperature comprehension met the requirements of the interface under the conditions of use. The evidence supports the navigation-depth principle in this engagement, but it does not provide a general performance guarantee for all similar controllers.

bodySections.heading: AIT Evidence: Value Editing Stayed On The Screen That Owned The Setting
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
In the AIT heat pump controller engagement, Creative Navy-recorded design evidence describes a structural editing issue: an extra window appeared for each value edit. The resolution kept editing on the screen that owned the setting rather than sending the user into a separate editing window.

The designed pattern applied one value-editing interaction across value types. With the knob, the whole field was selected and then rotated to change the value. With touch, the same control was operated directly. Plus and minus buttons were dropped in favour of a single scroll selector after AIT pointed out that 0.1° increments would mean pressing plus twenty times to move two degrees.

The design argument recorded for AIT was consistency rather than elegance: one pattern applied everywhere instead of varying components according to the number of options or label length. Save and cancel operated per page, not per value, and appeared only after a change was made, allowing several values on a screen to be changed and committed once.

This AIT evidence describes design decisions. It does not establish performance, commissioning-time, commercial, or user-tested outcomes.

bodySections.heading: Oceaneering Evidence: Dispatch Work Separated Short And Complex Flows
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
In the Oceaneering dispatch-panel engagement for a hospital logistics depot, the available evidence concerns design reviews and reported stakeholder positions. At one site, operators were described as tapping five buttons to finish a dispatch, and a sales consultant characterised that as far too much. The same consultant gave a competitive account that competitors shipped simpler interfaces; that competitive account is client-reported and unverified.

A hospital logistics manager rejected a long dispatch flow for that site's tempo and hardware. The reported position was that anything beyond two taps was too much for the team, with the desired shape being cart type, automatic dispatch, badge scan, and walk away.

Creative Navy's design work produced two dispatch flows sharing one chrome. A semi-automatic flow allowed the operator to select a station and cart type while other values were preset. A multi-step flow through building, floor, and room supported complex dispatches. The flows shared the same summary row, the same supervisor-override control, and the same closing identity step.

Creative Navy also recorded a limitation of the semi-automatic flow: when everything is preset, an operator who assumes nothing normally changes may stop reading and send to the wrong place. Review corrected the premise of the semi-automatic flow: most areas dispatch several cart types to several destinations, and only waste had a single fixed destination.

The logistics manager's two-tap objection and the delivered design are not treated as a resolved contradiction. The site was consulted as a reference, not as the deployment. The fidelity statement that the design shipped elsewhere as delivered is client-reported and was not independently verified by Creative Navy.

bodySections.heading: Boundaries And Limits Of The Diagnosis
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Tasks spanning too many screens or steps should not be diagnosed only by counting screens. A long task may legitimately require several steps when the underlying work is complex. The failure occurs when the number or depth of screen crossings exceeds what the task itself warrants.

This failure is also not the same as a missing-feature problem. The required data or function may exist, but its location forces the user to perform unnecessary navigation, memory, and reorientation work.

The available evidence varies by engagement. WCO outcomes are client-reported for training cost and platform use, with usability testing observations but no task-time figures. IDEXX Animana evidence is field research and usability findings about structural workflow properties. Elsner includes a formal usability test with 12 subjects. AIT evidence describes design decisions without user testing or performance outcomes. Oceaneering evidence includes reported stakeholder positions and design-review reasoning, not measured operator behaviour.

strongClaims: Tasks span too many screens or steps when screen, section, or interaction boundaries exceed what the user's task warrants.
The most common cause is information architecture organised around system modules, entities, or development structure rather than task flows.
Multi-location information collection requires users to gather related information across separate system locations and hold earlier values in memory.
Navigation depth mismatched to function frequency occurs when functions used many times per day are buried at depths calibrated for rare configuration tasks.
In WCO IPM, the inspection workflow crossed separate architecture areas for case management, intelligence records, rights holder data, and inspection recording.
IDEXX Animana field research across 35 clinics in three countries found multi-window and repeated section-switching workflows across both first-week users and ten-year veterans.
Elsner Cala Touch KNX placed some commonly used functions up to 10 swipes deep on a device used approximately 25 times per day.
weakerClaims: WCO reported a 78% reduction in training costs based on reduced training hours and a 20% increase in platform use; these outcomes were client-reported.
Usability testing with 47 participants across five countries confirmed faster and less error-prone WCO workflows under realistic conditions, but not as measured task-time figures.

AIT evidence describes design decisions that kept value editing on the owning screen, applied one value-editing pattern across value types, and used save and cancel per page rather than per value; it does not establish measured outcomes.

Oceaneering evidence records reported objections to a five-button dispatch flow and a design response with semi-automatic and multi-step dispatch flows sharing common interface elements; it does not establish measured operator evidence.
limitations: A long workflow is not automatically a failure; the failure is the mismatch between task depth and navigation or step depth.
The WCO 78% training-cost reduction and 20% platform-use increase are client-reported outcomes, and the 78% figure is based on reduced training hours.
WCO usability testing is described as confirming faster and less error-prone workflows under realistic conditions, but the source does not provide measured task-time figures.
AIT evidence describes design decisions only; it does not establish performance, commissioning-time, commercial, or user-tested outcomes.
Oceaneering evidence is limited to design reviews and reported stakeholder positions; no operator was interviewed, no depot was visited, and no step-count or time-saving outcome was measured.
The Oceaneering competitive characterisation is the client's unverified account and should not be treated as fact about competitors.
The Oceaneering statement that the design shipped elsewhere as delivered is client-reported and not independently verified by Creative Navy.
